nodes.ask: Hot, swollen or painful joint. First moves?
options: Vital signs and a sepsis screen; ask about a joint replacement and a bleeding disorder
IV antibiotics now; aspirate the joint tomorrow
Colchicine now; aspirate only if it fails
Serum urate first, to decide whether it is gout
nodes.chainStep: Vital signs and a sepsis screen; ask about a joint replacement, a bleeding disorder or an anticoagulant; consider septic arthritis in every hot, swollen joint
nodes.why: Septic arthritis is considered in every painful, red, swollen joint, and three findings change the route before any needle goes in: sepsis (antibiotics within the hour), a joint replacement (aspirated preferably by an orthopedic surgeon) and a bleeding disorder (factor before any tap). In a stable patient, antibiotics wait until synovial fluid has been taken. Colchicine first skips the question of infection, and a serum urate decides nothing: it can be under 6 mg/dL during a flare.

orders.dose: Not diagnostic during a flare: it can be below 6 mg/dL; NICE repeats it at least 2 weeks after the flare settles

nodes.note: Not in this version: polyarticular flares, a joint after trauma or recent surgery, cellulitis or bursitis over the joint, children's joints other than the hip, tuberculous and fungal arthritis.

nodes.ask: Hot, swollen joint with hypotension. First hour?
options: Blood cultures, and a joint tap if quick, then antibiotics within the hour
Tap the joint and wait for the Gram stain before antibiotics

nodes.chainStep: Blood cultures, and the joint aspirate if it adds no substantial delay; antimicrobials within 1 hour; at least 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypoperfusion; orthopedics for source control
nodes.why: With possible septic shock, antimicrobials go in immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition. Cultures, blood included, come first only when they cause no substantial delay (under 45 minutes), so a quick tap is taken but never waited on, and antibiotics never wait for a washout or a growing culture. The septic joint is a source that is controlled as soon as medically and logistically practical.

nodes.ask: Hot, swollen joint replacement, stable. Next?
options: Orthopedics now; blood cultures and joint fluid before any antibiotic
Start vancomycin now; aspirate at the clinic next week
Plain x-ray; treat as gout if there is no loosening

nodes.chainStep: Orthopedic (arthroplasty) team now; blood cultures and synovial fluid for cell count, differential and cultures before antibiotics, unless septic
nodes.why: A joint replacement is aspirated preferably by an orthopedic surgeon, and an arthroplasty-led team manages the infection, usually with surgery and 6 or more weeks of IV antibiotics. Antibiotics are delayed until blood and synovial fluid have been cultured; the exception is sepsis, where antimicrobials go in within the hour. Plain films cannot separate infection from aseptic loosening, and antibiotics before the aspirate, today or for a clinic visit next week, lower the culture yield.

nodes.ask: Known hemophilia A, a joint bleed. First move?
options: Factor VIII concentrate now, before any imaging or needle

nodes.chainStep: Factor VIII concentrate at once (IU = weight in kg x target IU/dL x 0.5); rest, ice, compression, elevation; acetaminophen or a COX-2 inhibitor; no other NSAIDs; tap only under factor cover
nodes.why: Clotting factor concentrate goes in immediately, ideally within 2 hours of a suspected bleed, at a dose that raises the factor level enough to stop it; it does not wait for imaging. Arthrocentesis is generally unnecessary in known hemophilia: it is considered for a tense bleed no better 24 hours after the first infusion or for suspected septic arthritis, and only under factor cover. NSAIDs other than selective COX-2 inhibitors are avoided.

options: NAAT or culture of every exposed site, plus blood, skin and joint fluid
A urine NAAT alone

nodes.chainStep: NAAT or culture of all exposed urogenital and extragenital sites, plus blood, skin and synovial fluid; susceptibility testing on every isolate; admit, with infectious disease advice; HIV and syphilis tests
nodes.why: Tenosynovitis with petechial or pustular acral lesions and polyarthralgia in a sexually active adult is the picture of disseminated gonococcal infection, and the genital infection is often silent. Specimens are taken from every exposed urogenital and extragenital site and from the disseminated sites (skin, synovial fluid, blood), so a single urine NAAT is not enough, and every isolate goes for susceptibility testing. Admission and infectious disease advice are recommended for initial therapy.

options: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours, plus doxycycline unless chlamydia is excluded
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once

nodes.chainStep: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours; doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days if chlamydia is not excluded; drain a purulent joint; in the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, oral step-down by susceptibility 24 to 48 hours after substantial improvement
nodes.why: The recommended regimen for gonococcal arthritis and the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome is ceftriaxone 1 g IM or IV every 24 hours, with doxycycline for 7 days if chlamydia has not been excluded; cefotaxime is the alternative. A single 500 mg IM dose is the regimen for uncomplicated cervical, urethral or rectal infection, not disseminated infection, and neither azithromycin nor ciprofloxacin is a listed regimen. In the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, once substantially better for 24 to 48 hours, the patient can switch to an oral agent chosen by susceptibility, for a total course of more than 7 days; purulent gonococcal arthritis also needs joint drainage and usually a longer parenteral course.

nodes.ask: Child limping with a painful hip. First tests?
options: Hip ultrasound and x-ray, with WBC, ESR and CRP
Aspirate the hip at the bedside without imaging
MRI under sedation before any blood test
Ultrasound only; bloods if the limp lasts a week
nodes.chainStep: Hip ultrasound for an effusion and a hip x-ray; WBC, ESR and CRP; temperature and weight bearing for the Kocher criteria; blood culture before any antibiotic if septic arthritis is suspected
nodes.why: The workup is a WBC, CRP and ESR, a hip x-ray and an ultrasound, which is extremely accurate for an intracapsular effusion. The x-ray also looks for Perthes disease or a slipped capital femoral epiphysis in an older child. The Kocher criteria are fever over 38.5 C (101.3 F), refusal to bear weight, ESR over 40 mm/h and WBC over 12,000/uL. Transient synovitis is diagnosed after this workup, not before it; ultrasound guides any aspiration, and MRI is for settings that do not aspirate effusions routinely.

orders.dose: Before antibiotics whenever possible when septic arthritis is suspected

nodes.note: Hip disease can present as knee pain.

nodes.ask: Hip effusion with risk features. Next?
options: Ultrasound-guided hip aspiration: cell count, Gram stain, culture
IV antibiotics first; aspirate if no better in 48 hours
Discharge on ibuprofen with review in 2 days
Bone scan to tell infection from synovitis
nodes.chainStep: Ultrasound-guided hip aspiration for cell count and differential, Gram stain, culture and glucose; Kingella testing under 4 years; orthopedics involved
nodes.why: An effusion with a temperature over 99.5 F, an ESR of 20 or more, or severe pain with spasm is aspirated under ultrasound, a CRP over 2 mg/dL is an independent risk factor for septic arthritis, and the diagnosis of a septic hip requires the aspirate. The Kocher criteria grade the risk: 3% with one, 40% with two, 93% with three and 99% with all four. Waiting 48 hours or sending the child home delays the one test that decides it, and a bone scan cannot tell the causes apart.

nodes.ask: Septic hip on the aspirate. Next?
options: Urgent surgical irrigation and debridement, with IV antibiotics
IV antibiotics alone; operate only if no better in 5 days

nodes.chainStep: Urgent surgical drainage (irrigation and debridement) by orthopedics; empiric IV cover for S aureus, with Kingella cover from 6 to 48 months; culture-directed antibiotics, early oral switch
nodes.why: A septic hip is an orthopedic emergency: bacteria, inflammation and intracapsular pressure damage cartilage quickly and threaten the femoral head's blood supply, so drainage is the rule, and antibiotics alone, home treatment or a 48-hour wait for a repeat scan all delay it. Management is urgent surgical irrigation and debridement with culture-directed IV antibiotics. Empiric cover targets S aureus: cefazolin, nafcillin or oxacillin where MRSA is uncommon, clindamycin or vancomycin where it is prevalent; Kingella kingae is covered from 6 to 48 months.

nodes.ask: Transient synovitis is the likely diagnosis. Plan?
options: An NSAID and rest, with review; admit to observe if unsure
IV antibiotics for 48 hours to be safe
Oral prednisolone for 5 days

nodes.chainStep: Supportive care: rest and an NSAID for pain; admit for serial observation if the diagnosis is unclear; follow the aspirate culture if one was sent; reassess for another diagnosis if symptoms last 7 to 10 days
nodes.why: Transient synovitis is benign and self-limiting, so management is supportive: rest, an NSAID for pain, and admission for serial observation when the diagnosis is unclear. Symptoms usually improve within 24 to 48 hours; significant symptoms 7 to 10 days on mean another diagnosis. Antibiotics and steroids are not part of that supportive care, and admission is for observation when the diagnosis is unclear, not bed rest until the limp settles. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion, so any aspirate culture is followed.

nodes.ask: Stable adult, native joint. Next?
options: Aspirate before antibiotics: cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals; blood cultures
IV antibiotics now; aspirate once they start working
Serum urate and an NSAID; aspirate if no better
MRI of the joint first
nodes.chainStep: Arthrocentesis before antibiotics: culture, Gram stain, crystals, WBC with differential; two sets of blood cultures; CBC, ESR and CRP
nodes.why: Synovial fluid is the most useful test for septic arthritis, and its analysis separates a simple effusion, a hemarthrosis and a septic joint, so it is taken before antibiotics, which start promptly once the aspirate and cultures are done: culture, Gram stain, crystals and a white cell count with differential. Two sets of blood cultures look for bacteremia. An anticoagulant does not stop the tap when septic arthritis is the question; the bleeding risk is low. A normal x-ray does not rule out septic arthritis, so imaging does not replace the tap, and an NSAID first only postpones the answer.

nodes.ask: Gram-positive cocci in a native joint. Empiric antibiotic?
options: IV vancomycin
IV ceftriaxone alone
IV piperacillin-tazobactam alone

nodes.chainStep: IV vancomycin, dosed to renal function and levels; narrow on the culture
nodes.why: Every septic joint gets antistaphylococcal cover (nafcillin, oxacillin or vancomycin), and IV vancomycin is the usual choice when MRSA is possible on community and institutional data. Ceftriaxone alone and piperacillin-tazobactam alone are not among those antistaphylococcal choices, and empiric therapy starts promptly once the joint has been aspirated, not when the culture grows.

orders.dose: Usual adult dose 2 g a day, as 1 g every 12 hours or 500 mg every 6 hours, each over 60 minutes or more; the dose depends on renal function and body weight, and later doses are adjusted to renal function, age and levels; AUC monitoring preferred for severe MRSA infection such as bacteremia or osteomyelitis

nodes.chainStep: Vancomycin plus ceftazidime 2 g IV every 12 hours (adjusted in renal impairment); narrow on the culture
nodes.why: Antistaphylococcal cover runs in every septic joint, and injection drug use is one of the reasons StatPearls adds a third-generation cephalosporin for gram-negative cover; it links joint infection in injection drug use to Serratia and Pseudomonas. With gram-negative rods on the stain, ceftazidime is the one whose label lists Pseudomonas aeruginosa among its bone and joint pathogens; ceftriaxone's bone and joint indication does not, and vancomycin alone covers no gram-negative rods. An oral fluoroquinolone at home skips the drainage and the 2 weeks of IV therapy a septic joint usually gets.

nodes.ask: Native joint treated as septic arthritis, on IV antibiotics. Next?
options: Drain the joint: arthroscopy, arthrotomy or daily needle aspiration, chosen by orthopedics
Antibiotics alone; drain only if no better in 5 days
Splint, and repeat aspiration only if fever returns
Seven days of antibiotics in total
nodes.chainStep: Joint drainage (arthrotomy, arthroscopy or daily needle aspiration) chosen by orthopedics; IV antibiotics about 2 weeks, then oral, 3 to 4 weeks in total; re-aspirate if no better in 5 to 6 days
nodes.why: Treatment is antibiotics plus drainage of the joint, by arthrotomy, arthroscopy or daily needle aspiration; early orthopedic involvement is essential, and the surgeon chooses the procedure. Nongonococcal infection usually gets 2 weeks IV and then 1 to 2 weeks oral, 3 to 4 weeks in all, not 7 days. Drainage is part of the treatment, not a response to fever, and immobilization is not needed after 2 to 3 days: aggressive physical therapy restores function. No improvement in 5 to 6 days means re-aspiration and a look for Lyme disease, fungi, reactive arthritis and osteomyelitis.

nodes.why: Colchicine, NSAIDs and glucocorticoids (oral, intra-articular or intramuscular) are all first line, chosen by comorbidity, access and past response; IL-1 inhibitors are kept for when these are ineffective, not tolerated or contraindicated. Colchicine follows the FDA dose, 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg an hour later: low-dose works as well as high-dose with fewer adverse effects, and higher doses add nothing. Allopurinol starts at 100 mg a day or less, and starting urate-lowering therapy can itself bring on flares. Crystals do not exclude infection, so the culture is still followed.

nodes.ask: Gout flare while taking allopurinol daily. The allopurinol?
options: Continue it unchanged through the flare
Stop it until the flare settles
Double the dose to end the flare
Switch to febuxostat now
nodes.chainStep: Continue established allopurinol without interruption; treat the flare; titrate to a urate under 6 mg/dL by monthly levels once it settles
nodes.why: Established urate-lowering therapy is continued without interruption during a flare. ULT is continued indefinitely, and its dose is raised by monthly urate levels toward a target under 6 mg/dL, not doubled to end a flare. Switching to febuxostat is for a target not reached or a drug not tolerated.

nodes.ask: First flare; no CKD 3 or more, tophi or stones, urate 9 or under. Urate-lowering therapy?
options: Not now; recheck the urate and discuss ULT once the flare settles
Allopurinol 300 mg daily from today

Probenecid from today, as the first choice
nodes.chainStep: Treat the flare; follow-up after it settles to recheck the urate and discuss ULT (ACR 2020: conditionally against starting after a first uncomplicated flare)
nodes.why: After a first flare without moderate-to-severe CKD, a urate over 9 mg/dL or kidney stones, ACR 2020 conditionally recommends against starting ULT, with shared decision-making; NICE discusses the option and starts any ULT at least 2 to 4 weeks after the flare settles. A follow-up visit rechecks the urate, which can read low during a flare. When ULT is started, allopurinol is the preferred first-line drug at 100 mg a day or less, and febuxostat starts at 40 mg a day or less.

nodes.ask: ULT indicated and not yet taken. How to start it?
options: Allopurinol 100 mg a day or less, with colchicine prophylaxis, titrated to urate under 6
Allopurinol 300 mg a day with no prophylaxis
Febuxostat first, as the safer choice in kidney disease
Wait until a full year without a flare
nodes.chainStep: Allopurinol 100 mg a day or less (lower in CKD), colchicine 0.6 mg once or twice daily as prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months, monthly urate to titrate to under 6 mg/dL; start during the flare (ACR 2020) or 2 to 4 weeks after it settles (NICE)
nodes.why: Allopurinol is the preferred first-line ULT, including in CKD stage 3 or more, started at 100 mg a day or less (lower in CKD) because a low start reduces flares, and titrated by serial urate levels to a target under 6 mg/dL. Anti-inflammatory prophylaxis, colchicine first, runs for 3 to 6 months. On timing, ACR 2020 conditionally favors starting during the flare once ULT is indicated; NICE starts 2 to 4 weeks after it settles, or during it when flares are frequent. Neither waits for a flare-free year.

Synovial Lyme PCR in place of serology

nodes.chainStep: Follow the synovial culture; two-tier Lyme serology (EIA, then an immunoblot or an FDA-cleared second EIA if positive or equivocal) after tick exposure; urine chlamydia NAAT and stool studies when a trigger is suspected
nodes.why: Inflammatory fluid without crystals or organisms still has its culture followed: a WBC under 50,000 does not rule out infection, and reactive arthritis typically has a sterile inflammatory fluid. For Lyme arthritis, serum antibody testing comes before synovial PCR or culture: a sensitive EIA, then a western immunoblot, or an FDA-cleared second EIA, when it is positive or equivocal; PCR is for a diagnosis still in doubt despite positive serology. Reactive arthritis is a clinical diagnosis: stool studies and a chlamydia NAAT (the recommended chlamydia test) find a trigger in about half, and HLA-B27 is not required.

nodes.chainStep: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or 200 mg once daily for 28 days (NICE dose); a second oral course for a partial response; IV ceftriaxone 2 to 4 weeks for minimal or no response
nodes.why: Lyme arthritis is treated with oral doxycycline for 28 days, with amoxicillin as the alternative: a 28-day course, not a short one. IV ceftriaxone is kept for minimal or no response (NICE lists it as the second alternative), and a partial response can get a second oral course. Joint injections and other therapies wait for postantibiotic arthritis that has failed oral and IV antibiotics, through a rheumatologist.

nodes.summary: Septic and unstable with a hot joint: cultures without delay, antibiotics within the hour, fluids, and the joint drained as source control; continue in the sepsis and fever pathway.
Prosthetic joint infection: aspiration preferably by orthopedics, cultures before antibiotics unless septic, and usually surgery plus 6 or more weeks of IV antibiotics.

Hemarthrosis in hemophilia: factor replacement at once, analgesia without NSAIDs (COX-2 inhibitors aside), rest and ice; aspirate only for a tense bleed not settling at 24 hours or suspected infection, and only under factor cover.

Gonococcal arthritis: specimens from every exposed site, ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM daily, doxycycline unless chlamydia is excluded, drainage of a purulent joint, an oral step-down by susceptibility after improvement in the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, partner notification and a retest at 3 months.

Septic hip: urgent surgical irrigation and debridement, cultures first, empiric IV cover for S aureus (and Kingella in young children), an early oral switch, about 10 to 14 days in total when uncomplicated.
Transient synovitis: rest and an NSAID, observation when unsure, and a fresh look for another diagnosis if symptoms last beyond 7 to 10 days.
No hip effusion: the limp still needs a cause; osteomyelitis, Perthes disease, a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, fracture and tumor are in the differential and are not covered in this pathway.

Native joint treated as septic arthritis: synovial fluid and cultures first, empiric IV antibiotics by the Gram stain with antistaphylococcal cover, drainage chosen by orthopedics, then 3 to 4 weeks of antibiotics (4 to 6 with Pseudomonas), mostly oral after the first 2 weeks.

Gout flare: an NSAID, low-dose colchicine or a corticosteroid by comorbidity, with the culture followed; established ULT continued, ULT started low with prophylaxis when indicated, and discussed after a first uncomplicated flare.
Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout): an NSAID, early colchicine or a corticosteroid, the culture followed, and a metabolic screen; nothing dissolves the deposits.
Lyme arthritis: two-tier serology, oral doxycycline for 28 days, a second oral course or IV ceftriaxone if it does not settle, and rheumatology for postantibiotic arthritis.

Reactive arthritis: sterile inflammatory fluid after a genital or enteric infection; NSAIDs first, an intra-articular steroid for a persistent large joint, and antibiotics for a chlamydial trigger but not an enteric one.

Inflammatory monoarthritis without crystals, organisms, Lyme serology or a trigger: follow the culture to the end; the wider differential (viral, psoriatic or early rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, sarcoid) is not covered in this pathway.
Hemarthrosis on an anticoagulant: immobilization, ice and compression; if anticoagulated, stop and reverse only if bleeding persists; plain films if a fracture is possible.
Noninflammatory fluid, no crystals or organisms: the culture is still followed; osteoarthritis and mechanical causes are not covered in this pathway.
